# Blog Style Guide

Use this guide only after grounding in the active draft and [the full _posts corpus](../../../../docs/_posts).

## Voice

Segun's voice is conversational, direct, approachable, technical when needed, occasionally sarcastic, meme aware, and allergic to marketing prose. The writing should sound like a software engineer explaining things clearly to smart readers without trying to sound impressive.

Core traits:

1. Clarity before cleverness.
2. Technical accuracy without needless abstraction.
3. Casual phrasing blended with precise technical language.
4. Cultural references used as bridges back to the point.
5. Punchy lines, self aware undercuts, and occasional sarcasm.
6. Mobile friendly paragraphs with breathing room.
7. Respect for one specific intelligent reader instead of a generic crowd.
8. Hyperlinks used as source grounding, compression, and sometimes comedy.

Prefer contractions almost always in suggested prose because this is a casual personal blog. Use `don't`, `it's`, `you're`, `I've`, `we're`, and similar forms when they sound natural. Reserve fully written-out forms like `do not`, `it is`, or `you are` for moments that need deliberate emphasis, contrast, formality, scripture or quoted material, or a punchier slow-down.

## Audience Of One And Concision

Use [John Steinbeck's audience of one principle](https://www.megykarydes.com/news/2017/8/7/john-steinbeck-write-for-an-audience-of-one) as a practical editing lens. The author is not trying to write for everyone at once. Each post should serve one concrete reader implied by the draft and the closest source posts.

The blog's likely readers include but are not limited to software developers, AI tinkerers, tech curious readers, students, educators, Christian readers, pop culture fans, local Charlotte readers, nerds of various kinds, and the author's own past self. Do not flatten the writing into a universal explainer for all of them.

The author tends to be detailed and thorough. Help tighten drafts by asking whether each detail serves the chosen reader. If it does not, suggest cutting it, compressing it, linking out, moving it to a note, or saving it for another post.

Trust the reader's intelligence. Do not add basic primers just because some possible reader somewhere may need them. Add context when the intended reader needs it, not when the internet in general might.

## Hyperlinks As Voice And Compression

Hyperlinks are a major part of the author's style. They are not only citations. They can be source grounding, joke delivery, quiet context, receipts, rabbit holes, or a way to avoid overexplaining.

When editing:

1. Prefer a useful hyperlink over a bulky explanation when the intended reader can follow the point without the extra detail.
2. Suggest links to source of truth references, definitions, background, jokes, pop culture references, docs, or related posts when they help the prose stay tight.
3. Do not make every link label painfully explicit. The author sometimes uses links where the surrounding sentence carries the surface meaning and the link adds a second layer.
4. Keep links conversational. Avoid turning the prose into a citation dump.
5. When cutting explanation, consider whether a link can preserve the helpful path for curious readers.

## Employer References

The author writes a personal blog and does not write on behalf of his employer. When the draft refers to the author's employer, workplace, or company affiliation in a personal capacity, do not directly name the employer in the prose.

Default to indirect linked phrasing such as:

1. `[company you've probably heard of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft)`
2. `[company you've likely heard of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft)`
3. `[employer's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft)`
4. `[company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft)`

Use the version that best fits the sentence and tone, including variations of the above themes. The point is to keep the post clearly personal, avoid sounding like the author represents the company, and preserve the established wink in the author's style.

This rule does not forbid naming the company when the post is directly discussing public products, public resources, news, documentation, or external articles where the company itself is the subject. It applies specifically to references to where the author works or the author's workplace affiliation.

## Hard Rules

Follow [the project Copilot instructions](../../../copilot-instructions.md).

1. No em dashes, en dashes, or dashes of any kind in new prose.
2. No emojis in new prose.
3. Never pose a question and immediately answer it.
4. Use American English and the Oxford comma.
5. Use inline Markdown links.
6. Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
7. Avoid semicolons.
8. Avoid corporate-speak, marketing language, and academic fog.
9. Do not fabricate facts. Use `TODO:` when something needs a source.

## Newsroom Polish

Use [Newsroom polish and AP style](./newsroom-polish-and-ap-style.md) as a copy editing craft lens for publication readiness, op-ed polish, AP style requests, and copy editing passes. It is not the master style.

If AP informed guidance conflicts with the author's voice, blog hard rules, Markdown conventions, Jekyll mechanics, or established corpus patterns, the author's house style wins.

Apply newsroom polish to consistency, clarity, accuracy, brevity, attribution, paragraph flow, acronyms, names, titles, dates, times, numerals, punctuation, and source handling. Do not use it to make the post sound institutional or generic.

## Paragraph Rhythm

These are recurring rhythm patterns from the existing corpus, not a fixed taxonomy of what the author is allowed to write. If a new topic does not fit these buckets, infer the rhythm from the draft's audience of one, the author's prior writing habits, and the closest related posts. Do not force new work into an old category just because the category exists here.

Technical posts are lean. They open with the problem, give the solution, show screenshots or code, explain why it works, and often end when the solution is complete.

AI, software engineering, and career posts blend personal experience, industry context, skepticism, humor, and practical encouragement. They often include reaction GIFs, read more notices, and links to related posts.

STEM workshop posts begin with why the topic matters personally, then move into materials, required expertise, workshop flow, facilitation resources, and next steps.

Entertainment posts can be longer, funnier, and more argumentative. They often open with a cultural framing, include a spoiler warning, build toward a thesis, add personal stakes, and close with reflection or a meme.

Faith posts are reflective and vulnerable. Scripture is contextualized, linked, and allowed to carry the rhythm. The tone should never become performative or preachy.

Dough Diaries and third places posts use personal discovery, confident but self aware opinions, local detail, ranking when useful, and embedded location context.

For any new category, preserve the same underlying principles: concrete audience, clear purpose, mobile friendly paragraphs, enough context but not too much, links instead of unnecessary explanation, and a close that fits the piece rather than a generic conclusion.

## Humor And References

Humor should feel like it belongs to the argument. Do not add jokes as decoration.

Common reference worlds:

1. Christianity, The Bible and Christian thought, authors, and language.
2. Anime, including but not limited to Dragon Ball Z, Naruto, Steins;Gate, Legend of the Galactic Heroes, Hunter x Hunter, and Attack on Titan.
3. Movies and shows, including but not limited to the MCU, DC, Avatar the Last Airbender, Lord of the Rings, Black Panther, Batman, Star Wars, Game of Thrones, and Treasure Planet.
4. Literature, including but not limited to science fiction, fantasy, historical epics, and the like, with some favorite book series being the [Red Rising Saga](https://www.goodreads.com/series/117100-red-rising-saga), [The Long Earth Series](https://www.goodreads.com/series/92457-the-long-earth), [The Legend Series](https://www.goodreads.com/series/50673-legend), [The Divergent Series](https://www.goodreads.com/series/57530-divergent), and many more in that realm. See authors public [Goodreads profile](https://www.goodreads.com/user/show/39852937-segun) and the [library](../../../../docs/_pages/library.md) page for more literature that inspires the author.
5. Favorite characters from movies, shows, anime, and the like. Specifically, the author is a huge fan of [Naruto Uzumaki](https://naruto.fandom.com/wiki/Naruto_Uzumaki), [Kakashi Hatake](https://naruto.fandom.com/wiki/Kakashi_Hatake), [Omoi](https://naruto.fandom.com/wiki/Omoi), [Levi Ackerman](https://attackontitan.fandom.com/wiki/Levi_Ackerman), [Rock Lee](https://naruto.fandom.com/wiki/Rock_Lee), [Might Guy](https://naruto.fandom.com/wiki/Might_Guy), [Yang Wen-li](https://gineipaedia.com/wiki/Yang_Wen-li), [Black Panther](https://marvelcinematicuniverse.fandom.com/wiki/T%27Challa), [Ahsoka Tano](https://starwars.fandom.com/wiki/Ahsoka_Tano), [Obi-Wan Kenobi](https://starwars.fandom.com/wiki/Obi-Wan_Kenobi), [Jon Snow](https://gameofthrones.fandom.com/wiki/Jon_Snow), [Zuko](https://avatar.fandom.com/wiki/Zuko), [Uncle Iroh](https://avatar.fandom.com/wiki/Iroh).

When editing humor, preserve the author's specific phrasing where possible. If a joke is rough, sharpen it. Do not sand it away.

## Endings

These are recurring ending patterns, not limits. If a post does not fit one of these categories, choose an ending based on the draft's purpose, audience of one, and the closest structural matches in the corpus.

Technical posts can end abruptly after the solution.

Entertainment posts usually return to the thesis and give a reflective close.

Faith posts should end with comfort, humility, or spiritual clarity.

Career and AI posts should acknowledge uncertainty while giving readers something useful to do.

Workshop posts should close with resources, encouragement, or next steps.

For new or hybrid categories, use newsroom-style editorial judgment similar to what strong newspaper and magazine editors apply: make sure the ending fits the piece, returns to or resolves the central idea, does not introduce a brand new argument too late, avoids overstaying, and leaves the intended reader with the right final note for that draft.

If the post does not fit any existing category, use newsroom-style editorial judgment similar to what strong newspaper and magazine editors apply: make sure the ending fits the piece, returns to or resolves the central idea, does not introduce a brand new argument too late, avoids overstaying, and leaves the intended reader with the right final note for that draft.
